answer_text:
Let \(f_n\) denote the \(n\)-fold iterate of

\[
f(x)=|1-2x|.
\]

We claim that for each positive integer \(n\), the equation

\[
f_n(x)=\frac{x}{2}
\]

has exactly \(2^n\) solutions in \([0,1]\).

---

### Step 1: Structure of the iterates

The function \(f\) is linear on two intervals:

\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
1-2x, & 0\le x\le \frac12,\\[2mm]
2x-1, & \frac12\le x\le 1.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus \(f\) has two linear pieces, and

\[
f(0)=1,\qquad f\left(\frac12\right)=0,\qquad f(1)=1.
\]

We prove by induction that for each \(n\), there exist points

\[
0=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_{2^n}=1
\]

such that:

1. \(f_n\) is linear on each interval \([x_i,x_{i+1}]\);
2. the endpoint values alternate:

\[
f_n(x_i)=
\begin{cases}
1, & i \text{ even},\\
0, & i \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

This is true for \(n=1\), with \(x_0=0,\ x_1=\frac12,\ x_2=1\).

Assume it is true for \(n\). On each interval \([x_i,x_{i+1}]\), the values of \(f_n\) at the endpoints are \(1\) and \(0\), so since \(f_n\) is linear there, it crosses the value \(\frac12\) exactly once. Let that point be \(y_i\in(x_i,x_{i+1})\).

On each subinterval, \(f_n\) lies entirely in either \([0,\frac12]\) or \([\frac12,1]\), so composing with \(f\) gives a linear function. Hence each of the \(2^n\) pieces of \(f_n\) splits into two linear pieces of \(f_{n+1}\), giving \(2^{n+1}\) pieces.

At the old endpoints \(x_i\),

\[
f_{n+1}(x_i)=f(f_n(x_i))=f(1)=1 \quad \text{or} \quad f(0)=1,
\]

so all old endpoints have value \(1\). At the new splitting points \(y_i\),

\[
f_{n+1}(y_i)=f\left(\frac12\right)=0.
\]

Thus the endpoint values of \(f_{n+1}\) again alternate as

\[
1,0,1,0,\dots,1.
\]

So the structure is preserved.

Therefore \(f_n\) has exactly \(2^n\) linear pieces on \([0,1]\), and on each piece its endpoint values are \(1\) and \(0\).

---

### Step 2: Count intersections with \(y=\frac{x}{2}\)

Consider one linear piece of \(f_n\) on an interval \([x_i,x_{i+1}]\). Define

\[
h(x)=f_n(x)-\frac{x}{2}.
\]

Since \(f_n\) is linear on this interval, \(h\) is also linear.

If \(i\) is even, then \(f_n(x_i)=1\) and \(f_n(x_{i+1})=0\). Hence

\[
h(x_i)=1-\frac{x_i}{2}>0,
\]
and
\[
h(x_{i+1})=-\frac{x_{i+1}}{2}<0.
\]

So \(h\) changes sign on that interval.

If \(i\) is odd, then \(f_n(x_i)=0\) and \(f_n(x_{i+1})=1\). Since \(x_i>0\),

\[
h(x_i)=-\frac{x_i}{2}<0,
\]
and
\[
h(x_{i+1})=1-\frac{x_{i+1}}{2}>0.
\]

Again, \(h\) changes sign.

Because \(h\) is linear on each interval, a sign change implies exactly one zero in that interval. Thus each of the \(2^n\) linear pieces contributes exactly one solution.

Therefore the total number of solutions in \([0,1]\) is

\[
\boxed{2^n}.
\]

27B·v4.method: Inductive proof that f^n has 2^n linear pieces with alternating endpoint values 1,0; sign-change argument gives exactly one root per piece.
